title: Both sides, every time
setting: A junior accountant has recorded the same thing twice.

lines.t: I've posted an entry twice by mistake.
Then post a reversing journal entry. Never delete anything in the general ledger.
Why not simply remove it?
Because the history has to show what happened. Bookkeeping is a record, and records don't get tidied.
Which side does the payment go on?
Money arriving in the bank account is a debit there. The credit goes to the customer's account.
Double-entry still confuses me after three months.
Everything is written twice, in two places, and the two have to agree. That's the whole idea.
And where do I find the right account code?
The chart of accounts. Print it, keep it beside you, and in a month you'll know the ones you use daily.
How many are there?
Two hundred. You'll use eleven.

title: Close by the fifth
setting: The monthly accounts always arrive too late to be useful.

lines.t: Month-end close has to finish by the fifth working day.
We've never managed it before the ninth.
Which is why the management accounts arrive when nobody can act on them.
What holds it up?
The trial balance. Two cost centres never post on time.
Marketing and the Varna site.
Then chase those two on the second, instead of the seventh.
And the variance report?
Plan against actual, by cost centre, on one page. Anything over 10% gets a sentence explaining it.
Gross profit is up and net profit is flat again.
That's the line the owner stops at. EBITDA looks kinder, and he'll ask why we show both.
Because the interest on the loan is real money.
Exactly. Capex belongs in the year-end report. Opex belongs in every single month.

title: Forty-eight euro
setting: A supervisor asks a bookkeeper not to write off a small difference.

lines.t: The bank reconciliation is out by forty-eight euro. Everything else matches.
What were you going to do with it?
Post an adjustment. It's below materiality and it's Friday.
Give it thirty minutes first. Where does the forty-eight come from?
A courier charge. It's in the purchase ledger and in office costs.
So it's a duplicate. Have you looked for others from that supplier?
Not yet. Give me a moment... there are eleven more across the year.
Which means costs are overstated and profit is understated.
One thousand three hundred and forty euro in total.
Small differences are rarely small. Write a note for the file.

title: Eleven leva
setting: A small difference that somebody wants to round away.

lines.t: The bank reconciliation is out by eleven leva.
In which direction?
We show eleven more than the bank does.
Then something was recorded twice, or a fee wasn't recorded at all.
It's eleven leva. Can I not just adjust it?
No. A discrepancy of eleven today is a discrepancy of eleven thousand in June, and you'll have no idea where it began.
So I go through the statement line by line.
Start with last week, and look for two identical amounts.
Found it. A card fee posted twice.
Good. Reconcile it properly and we balance the books without anybody inventing a number.

title: Ninety days and counting
setting: Three customers have stopped paying and one of them has a point.

lines.t: Print the aged debtors report before the meeting.
Three customers are over ninety days.
Which is where credit control stops being polite.
One of them disputes the amount. He says we charged for a delivery he refused.
If he's right, issue a credit note today and stop arguing about it.
And the other two?
Phone calls. An email is very easy to leave unopened.
The one from Ruse looks like a bad debt.
It probably is. We don't write it off while there's still an address and a phone number.
I'll update the sales ledger after each call so the report is true tomorrow morning.

title: Why December looks bad
setting: Explaining non-cash adjustments to a director.

lines.t: November showed nine thousand profit. December shows almost nothing.
Three things landed in December, and none of them are cash.
Go on.
The annual insurance was posted in full instead of as a prepayment.
So it should be spread over twelve months.
Yes. Second, a provision for the disputed invoice.
And the third?
Depreciation on the new equipment started. Seven hundred a month.
So the bank balance is actually fine.
Higher than November. Always ask what moved that isn't cash.

title: The insurance paid in January
setting: Costs that happened in one month and were paid in another.

lines.t: We paid the whole year's insurance in January.
Then it's a prepayment. One twelfth belongs to each month.
So January doesn't carry the whole cost.
On a cash basis it would. We use accruals, so a cost sits in the month it covers.
What about the electricity bill that hasn't arrived?
Put in an accrual for the estimate. The electricity was used in March whether the paper turned up or not.
And the van?
Depreciation over five years. The software licence gets amortisation over three.
The court case the lawyer mentioned?
A provision, if it's likely and we can estimate it. Merely possible isn't enough.
And the old stock in the back room?
A write-down to what it's actually worth. Whatever is left we carry forward into next year and look at it again.

title: What we own by Friday
setting: The bank has asked for a list of everything the company owns and owes.

lines.t: The bank wants a list of what we own and what we owe.
Start with the fixed assets?
Vans, machines, the kitchen. Everything we use for years.
At what value?
Net book value. Original cost, minus the depreciation so far.
And the stock?
That's a current asset, and the inventory valuation has to be honest. Nobody is paying full price for those 2019 boxes.
What counts as a current liability?
Anything due within a year. Supplier invoices, the VAT, the short part of the loan.
Then I'll build both lists from the ledger and mark anything I'm unsure about instead of guessing.

title: Forty leva and a coat pocket
setting: The cash box is short and somebody has the receipt at home.

lines.t: Petty cash is forty leva short.
Since when?
Since somebody bought biscuits and left the receipt in a coat pocket.
Then the coat comes back, or the money does. Either is fine.
It's forty leva.
It's forty leva every month for a year. Nobody notices until the auditor does.
Do I reimburse him without the receipt?
Once, with a note saying why. After that, no receipt, no payment.
And the supplier invoices?
Into the purchase ledger the day they arrive. A bill you haven't recorded is a surprise waiting for you.

title: Show me how you got there
setting: An auditor picks one number and follows it backwards.

lines.t: This figure here. Show me how you reached it.
There's an audit trail behind every number in that report.
Then take me from the total back to a single invoice.
Total, ledger, journal entry, invoice. Four steps, and the supporting documentation is scanned.
What about the eleven leva difference in March?
Below materiality, and documented anyway, because I'd rather explain it now than remember it in a year.
That's the right answer.
We follow the accounting standards on the accruals and I can show you the working for each one.
And the statutory accounts?
Filed on the 28th, three weeks early, for the first time in this company's history.
Then this will be a short audit.
